title: You Don’t Need to Prove Yourself
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: The Mindful Manager uses the clash between Jose Mourinho and captain Iker Casillas at Real Madrid, shown in a Netflix documentary, to examine how a capable new leader can go wrong when joining an existing team. The author argues that the difference between a great and a failed arrival is whether the leader brings people on board. The central mindset shift is between asking "What can I teach?" and "What can I learn?", since the urge to prove oneself leads new managers to talk more than they listen and to change things too early. The piece then offers three practices: take time to understand what has been tried, what constraints exist and why, trust the quietly influential people who have earned respect, and stop comparing yourself with a predecessor. A personal story of leading a client service team abroad with a respected number two shows these ideas working. The author closes by asking leaders to choose deliberately between commanding authority and earning trust.
points: A new leader's first choice is between asking what they can teach and what they can learn, and that choice shapes the relationship with the team.
The urge to prove yourself tempts new managers to see fixes everywhere before they understand what has been tried or what constraints exist.
Informal authority sits with respected people who do not appear on the organisational chart, and winning their support makes later changes land far more smoothly.
Comparing yourself with a brilliant predecessor is neither useful nor fair; the task is to become the leader the team needs now.
Bringing people with you so that projects become "our projects" matters more than pushing through changes to make your own mark.
quotes: You can arrive with the best intentions and the most brilliant ideas in the world, but if your team isn’t with you, you’re going to struggle.
We can focus on understanding the team dynamics. Who commands authority, how decisions get made, what invisible lines there are in the organigram.
Because as a new manager, we’re walking into an existing social system, with its own relationships, loyalties, history, status and ways of doing things.
You can see what isn’t working. You don’t necessarily know why.
Good leadership in a new environment requires curiosity. It means asking questions that you could probably answer yourself, then listening carefully to the answers.
His influence might not have appeared on the organisational chart, but it made all the difference to how successfully I landed.
Your job isn’t to become your predecessor, it’s to become the leader this team needs now.
As a new leader, you can choose to command authority or earn trust. You can show people how brilliant you are or help them discover how brilliant they can be.
